diagnosis_explanation:
Your child has a stomach problem. It is called gastroenteritis. This means the stomach and gut are upset. Doctors are not sure if there is also a blockage in the gut. This is called a bowel obstruction.

Your child also has trouble with acid coming up from the stomach. This is called reflux. It is a big problem for your child. Your child sometimes throws up. This is likely from the stomach upset.

Your child has a condition called Goldenhar syndrome. This is something your child was born with. It can affect how the head and face grow. Your child also has low blood count. This is called anemia. It may be from not having enough iron.

Your child had trouble breathing in food or liquid before. This is called aspiration. It led to a lung problem called pneumonia. Doctors will watch your child closely.
medication_rationale:
Pepcid:
This medicine was given to help your child's stomach problems. It reduces the amount of acid in the stomach. Your child might not notice much as this medicine works. Some children get headaches. Your doctor wants you to watch for signs of a bad reaction. Call your doctor if your child has trouble breathing.

Reglan:
This medicine was given to help your child's bowels move more easily. This can help if your child has a blockage. Your child might feel less sick to their stomach. Some children get sleepy or dizzy. Watch for movements that are jerky or uncontrolled. Call your doctor if these happen or if your child gets a rash.
Important: Do not stop taking this medicine without calling your doctor first.
recovery_trajectory:
**Week 1:**
- Your child may feel uncomfortable and have a decreased appetite.
- Keep your child’s head elevated.
- Watch for increased redness or drainage around the G-tube.
- Make sure your child is taking their feeds through the G-tube and J-tube as directed.
- Your child’s goal this week is to tolerate feeds without spitting up.
- Call your doctor if your child has a fever over 100.4F.
- Call your doctor if your child seems more sleepy than usual.

**Week 2:**
- Your child may start to show more interest in feeding.
- Continue to feed your child as directed by the doctor.
- Monitor the G-tube site for any signs of infection.
- Watch for any changes in your child's breathing or stool.
- Your child’s goal this week is to have stable bowel sounds.
- Call your doctor if your child has vomiting or diarrhea.
- Call your doctor if your child’s tummy becomes very hard.

**Week 3:**
- Your child might show slightly more energy this week.
- Continue to follow the feeding plan for the G-tube and J-tube.
- Keep the area around the G-tube clean and dry.
- Ensure the dressing on the J-tube is clean and secure.
- Your child’s goal this week is to maintain a stable weight.
- Call your doctor if you see blood in your child's stool.
- Call your doctor if your child has trouble breathing.

**Week 4:**
- Your child may be able to tolerate slightly larger feeds.
- Continue with the prescribed tube feedings.
- Watch the G-tube site for any signs of irritation or leakage.
- Make sure your child’s bowel sounds are consistent.
- Your child’s goal this week is to show consistent signs of comfort during feeds.
- Call your doctor if your child develops a rash or skin irritation.
- Call your doctor if your child has any signs of poor feeding.

**When to expect improvement:**
- Improvement is usually seen over several weeks.
- Continue all prescribed tube feedings carefully.
- Monitor your child closely for any new symptoms.
- Follow up with your doctor as scheduled.
- Patience is key as your child recovers.
escalation_guide:
CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY
These symptoms are life-threatening. Do not drive yourself.
- Your child cannot breathe: This is an emergency. Call 911 now.
- Your child is unresponsive: Call 911 right away.
- Your child has a seizure: Call 911 at once.
- Your child is bleeding badly: Call 911 if it won't stop.
- Your child shows stroke signs: Face droops or arm weakness. Call 911 now.
- Your child has chest pain: Call 911 if it is severe.
- Your child has a severe allergic reaction: Call 911 if they can't breathe.

GO TO THE ER TODAY
Do not wait until tomorrow. Go within a few hours.
- Your child has a high fever: Over 101 degrees F. This needs care.
- Your child cannot keep fluids down: For 12 hours or more. They need fluids.
- Your child's belly is very hard: And they have bad pain. This needs checking.
- Your child has a wound with red streaks: Or pus. This looks infected.
- Your child has significant swelling in one leg: With pain. This could be a clot.
- Your child is very confused: Or not acting right. This is new.
- Your child fell hard: And may have hurt themselves.

CALL YOUR DOCTOR
Call during office hours. Do not go to the ER for these.
- Your child has mild pain: That is slowly getting better.
- Your child has mild nausea: Without any vomiting.
- Your child is healing slowly: But has no signs of infection.
- You have questions about medicine: Talk to your doctor's office.
